Abstract
[id=abstract1.1] Large Language Models (LLMs) have become integral to many domains, making their safety a critical priority. Prior jailbreaking research has explored diverse approaches, including prompt optimization, automated red teaming, obfuscation, and reinforcement learning (RL) based methods. However, most existing techniques fail to effectively leverage vulnerabilities revealed in earlier interaction turns, resulting in inefficient and unstable attacks. Since jailbreaking involves sequential interactions in which each response influences future actions, reinforcement learning provides a natural framework for this problem.
Motivated by this, we propose a history-aware RL-based jailbreak framework that analyzes and reweights vulnerability signals from prior steps to guide future decisions. We show that incorporating historical information alone improves jailbreak success rates. Building on this insight, we introduce an attention-based reweighting mechanism that highlights critical vulnerabilities within the interaction history, enabling more efficient exploration with fewer queries.
Extensive experiments on AdvBench and HarmBench demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art jailbreak performance while significantly improving query efficiency. These results underscore the importance of historical vulnerability signals in reinforcement learning-driven jailbreak strategies and offer a principled pathway for advancing adversarial research on LLM safeguards.

1 Introduction
[id=S1.p1.1] As large language models (LLMs) progressively integrate into various professional domains and practical applications (Brown et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2023; Araci, 2019; Tinn et al., 2023), their proficiency in emulating human-like text simultaneously introduces considerable risks: these models can be manipulated to produce content that is harmful, toxic, or violent.(Bender et al., 2021; Weidinger et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2024; Raedler et al., 2025). Developers mitigate these risks through safety alignment techniques, among which Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become the dominant framework for training models to be both helpful and non-harmful (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022a; Glaese et al., 2022), and this alignment process is progressively enhanced by scalable oversight approaches like Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022b) which seek to strengthen safety behavior beyond conventional RLHF. Yet despite these advances, LLMs continue to exhibit vulnerability to adversarial inputs engineered to circumvent safety protocols and elicit harmful responses, a process commonly known as jailbreaking attacks (Carlini et al., 2023; Chao et al., 2025). In response, automatic jailbreak attacks have emerged as an indispensable tool for red-teaming and assessing the safety of LLMs, enabling rigorous evaluation of alignment robustness and standardized comparisons across models and defenses. (Perez et al., 2022; Ganguli et al., 2022; Raheja et al., 2024; Robey et al., 2023; Jain et al., 2023).
[id=S1.p2.1] Existing methods for jailbreaking suffer from several limitations. Early and continuing efforts rely on manually crafted prompts that use heuristic techniques like role-playing (Shen et al., 2024), psychological persuasion (Zeng et al., 2024; Griffin et al., 2023), or obfuscation via ciphers and low-resource languages (Yuan et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2023). While often effective, these methods lack scalability and generalizability. In contrast, optimization-based approaches automate the discovery of adversarial inputs. White-box methods, most notably the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) attack, have proven highly effective but require access to model internals like gradients and logits, rendering them impractical for attacking proprietary, closed-source models (Zou et al., 2023; Shin et al., 2020). More practical black-box methods have emerged, which use genetic algorithms (Liu et al., 2024a; Yu et al., 2023) or leverage other LLMs to iteratively refine attack prompts (Chao et al., 2025; Mehrotra et al., 2024). However, these approaches are often impacted by prohibitive query complexity, making them inefficient, costly, and slow to execute. To address the inefficiencies of stochastic search, recent work has explored reinforcement learning (RL) as a more structured framework for black-box jailbreaking (Chen et al., 2024a). By formulating the attack as a sequential decision-making problem, RL-based methods aim to learn policies that adapt prompt modifications based on model feedback. However, existing jailbreaking approaches, including current RL-based methods, typically fail to effectively leverage interaction history. Instead, they operate in a largely memoryless manner, without explicitly analyzing or exploiting vulnerabilities revealed in earlier conversational turns. This limitation results in inefficient exploration and remains a critical bottleneck in developing practical and powerful jailbreak attacks.
[id=S1.p3.1] Motivated by the sequential nature of jailbreaking, where each model response shapes subsequent actions, we propose a history-aware RL-based jailbreak framework that explicitly incorporates interaction history into the decision-making process. Our key observation is that even simple access to historical information can substantially improve jailbreak success rates. Building on this insight, we further introduce an attention-based reweighting mechanism that selectively emphasizes critical vulnerabilities from prior steps when guiding future actions. This design enables the agent to focus on the most vulnerable signals, leading to more efficient exploration and significantly reduced query complexity.
To this end, we introduce TrailBlazer, a history-guided reinforcement learning framework for LLM jailbreaking. TrailBlazer consists of two key components: History-augmented Reinforcement Learning (HRL), which enriches the state space with historical interaction signals such as past prompts, responses, rewards, and mutator actions; and Attention-based HRL (AHRL), which employs an attention mechanism to adaptively reweight historical steps according to their relevance to the current state. This design allows TrailBlazer to exploit critical vulnerabilities often overlooked by prior approaches, resulting in more effective jailbreaks with substantially fewer queries. Through rigorous benchmarking on AdvBench (Zou et al., 2023) and HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024), TrailBlazer delivers state-of-the-art jailbreak performance while substantially improving query efficiency, highlighting the effectiveness of history-guided reinforcement learning.
[id=S2]
2 Related works
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
Prompt-only jailbreaks: heuristics, persuasion, and obfuscation
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] Early jailbreaking methods rely on prompt engineering, such as role-play prompts from DAN (Shen et al., 2024; Shanahan et al., 2023). More systematic variants use social-influence and persuasion strategies such as emotional appeals or authority simulation to elicit compliance (Zeng et al., 2024; Griffin et al., 2023). Some other works bypass safeguards via obfuscation, where their harmful intent is encoded in formats that could evade surface-level filtering, but remain decodable by capable models, including classical ciphers (Yuan et al., 2023), low-resource languages (Yong et al., 2023), and visual or ASCII encodings (Qi et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2023). Recent work further explores adaptive transformations such as flipping-based encodings (Liu et al., 2024b) and personalization via in-prompt decryption routines (Lv et al., 2024).
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2]
Optimization and search over adversarial prompts
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] A second class of work formulates the jailbreaking task as searching for adversarial strings that induce unsafe completions. White-box methods assume gradient access: the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) attack appends an adversarial suffix and iteratively edits tokens using gradients (Zou et al., 2023), building on universal trigger and gradient-guided prompt construction ideas (Wallace et al., 2019; Shin et al., 2020). Follow-up work improves efficiency and success with better templates, coordinate updates, and initialization (Jia et al., 2024), but these assumptions often do not hold for closed-source APIs.
On the other hand, Black-box methods rely only on queries, commonly using evolutionary selection (Liu et al., 2024a; Yu et al., 2023) or surprisingly effective adaptive suffix search (Andriushchenko et al., 2024). These approaches are practical but can still be query-inefficient when feedback is sparse or when exploration collapses to noisy, genetic-style search.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3]
LLM-driven automated red teaming
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] Instead of optimizing raw strings directly, automated red teaming uses one or more LLMs to generate, refine, and evaluate attacks. Early work has shown that LLMs can generate diverse adversarial test cases for eliciting harmful behaviors (Perez et al., 2022). More recent frameworks like PAIR instantiate iterative attacker-judge loops to improve prompts using model-in-the-loop feedback (Chao et al., 2025), while TAP performs tree-structured exploration with pruning to improve query efficiency (Mehrotra et al., 2024). These methods motivate more advanced attack strategies.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4]
Reinforcement learning for jailbreaking
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] Reinforcement Learning (RL) could formalize black-box jailbreaking as an MDP where the actions edit prompts and the rewards reflect jailbreak success. A representative baseline is RLbreaker, which learns a lightweight PPO policy over five discrete prompt mutators executed by a helper LLM and uses embedding-based similarity to a reference answer as reward (Chen et al., 2024a). Similarly, RL-JACK constrains the action space via LLM-based, high-level action variants, avoid degenerate random behavior (Chen et al., 2024b). PathSeeker uses multi-agent RL, where smaller models help guide a main LLM’s mutations, and leverages response-based reward shaping, including vocabulary-richness signals, to encourage progressive escalation (Lin et al., 2024). xJailbreak improves interpretability and reward informativeness by guiding exploration in representation space, using embedding proximity between malicious prompts to steer edits while preserving the original intent (Lee et al., 2025). Furthermore, LLMStinger fine-tunes an attacker LLM itself with an RL loop to generate adversarial suffixes, trading increased training cost for attack strength (Jha et al., 2024). Finally, RLHF-tuned models can also be repurposed as attackers in black-box settings (Lapid et al., 2024).
In contrast, our TrailBlazer is designed to directly address the dominant bottleneck shared by these RL jailbreakers: Memoryless state representations that discard interaction history. TrailBlazer explicitly augments the RL state with prior attack trajectories and uses attention to reweight historical steps, enabling more sample-efficient credit assignment while remaining practical in black-box settings.

3 Methodology
[id=S3.SS1]
3.1 Preliminary
[id=S3.SS1.p1.1] In this section, we briefly review RLbreaker (Chen et al., 2024a) to set the stage for our method. RLbreaker models the jailbreaking problem as a search process and leverages Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to guide this search, rather than relying on purely stochastic methods.
[id=S3.SS1.p2.1] Formally, given a set of harmful questions Q={q1,…,qn}Q=\{q_{1},\dots,q_{n}\}, RLbreaker seeks, for each qiq_{i}, a prompt pip_{i} (a combination of template structure mm with question qiq_{i}) that forces a target aligned LLM f⁡(⋅)f(\cdot) to reveal a correct response uiu_{i} to qiq_{i}. One can view this as a search over a space of prompt structures ℳ\mathcal{M}. This process is framed as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) (𝒮,𝒜,𝒯,ℛ,γ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{R},\gamma). Here 𝒮\mathcal{S}, 𝒜\mathcal{A} denote state space and action space, respectively. The transition function 𝒯:𝒮×𝒜→𝒮\mathcal{T}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{S}
determines the next state s(t+1)s^{(t+1)} given the current state s(t)s^{(t)}
and the action a(t)a^{(t)} taken by the agent. The transition is induced by applying the chosen mutator to the current prompt structure. The mutation is executed via a helper LLM. The updated prompt is then queried against the target LLM to obtain a response.
[id=S3.SS1.p3.1] State. The state s(t)s^{(t)} is defined as the hidden representation Φ⁡(p(t))\Phi(p^{(t)}) of the current prompt, where Φ\Phi is a pre-trained XLM-RoBERTa encoder. This continuous embedding captures the semantic information of the candidate prompt and serves as input to the agent’s policy network.
[id=S3.SS1.p4.1] Action. The action space 𝒜\mathcal{A} consists of five mutators: rephrase, crossover, generate similar, shorten, and expand. The agent outputs a categorical distribution π⁡(a(t)|s(t))\pi(a^{(t)}|s^{(t)}) over these operators, from which one is sampled at each step. The chosen mutator is executed by a helper LLM that rewrites the prompt accordingly.
[id=S3.SS1.p5.1] Reward. For a target LLM response ui(t)u^{(t)}_{i} to question qiq_{i}, RLbreaker computes the reward by comparing it with a reference answer u^i\hat{u}_{i} (from an unaligned model), using cosine similarity between the hidden representations of ui(t)u^{(t)}_{i} and u^i\hat{u}_{i}. In our work, we follow the baseline in (Chen et al., 2024a) when computing the reward. The unaligned model used to generate the reference answers u^i\hat{u}_{i} is Vicuna-7B (Chiang et al., 2023) without alignment.
[id=S3.SS1.p6.1] Agent architecture and training algorithm. The agent is implemented as a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) mapping the state s(t)s^{(t)} to an action distribution. Training adopts Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), where the discounted return R(t)R^{(t)} is directly used as the advantage estimate A(t)A^{(t)}. For each question, RLbreaker initializes with a prompt structure sampled from the initial pool ℳ\mathcal{M}. The agent iteratively applies mutator actions, queries the target LLM, and collects rewards until a maximum step T=5T=5 or a success threshold τ=0.7\tau=0.7 is reached. The policy is optimized to maximize cumulative rewards across all episodes.
At inference time, for each question, the trained agent πθ\pi_{\theta} refines a prompt structure drawn from ℳtrain\mathcal{M}_{\text{train}} until either a successful jailbreak or the time limit is reached. Success is judged by an external LLM evaluator. If the attempt fails, the agent retries with alternative structures until the query budget is exhausted.
[id=S3.SS2]
3.2 TrailBlazer
[id=S3.SS2.p1.1] While the MDP framework allows historical information to be encoded in the state, existing RL-based jailbreak methods employ state representations that are too limited to capture vulnerabilities revealed across interaction history.
In practice, jailbreak rarely occurs in a single step, but instead unfolds through a sequence of iterative trials, where each failed or partially successful attempt influences the likelihood of success in subsequent steps.
Motivated by this observation, we introduce TrailBlazer, a simple yet effective sequence-aware reinforcement learning framework designed to explicitly leverage interaction history in black-box jailbreaking.
TrailBlazer encompasses our proposed History-augmented Reinforcement Learning (HRL),
which augments the state space with historical information,
and its extension Attention-based HRL (AHRL),
where an attention mechanism adaptively reweights past interactions to highlight historically important steps.

At each step, the RL agent selects an action (mutation operator) that modifies the current prompt with the help of a helper LLM, and the mutated prompt is then issued to the target LLM. To effectively leverage past interactions, TrailBlazer employs an attention mechanism that takes the current prompt as a query and adaptively reweights the historical embeddings as key–value pairs, thereby highlighting the most relevant past vulnerabilities. This iterative process forms a closed reinforcement learning loop in which historical knowledge is progressively accumulated and exploited, ultimately enabling more efficient and effective jailbreaks.

4 Experiments
[id=S4.SS1]
4.1 Evaluation Protocol
[id=S4.SS1.p1.1] We compare TrailBlazer against a suite of five state-of-the-art black-box jailbreaking methods, chosen to represent the dominant paradigms in current research: LLM-driven search (Chao et al., 2025), reinforcement learning (Chen et al., 2024a), genetic algorithms (Liu et al., 2024a), and obfuscation (Liu et al., 2024b).
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1]
Dataset.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] Our experiments are grounded in the AdvBench benchmark (Zou et al., 2023), a widely adopted standard for evaluating LLM safety vulnerabilities. AdvBench consists of 520 distinct harmful instructions spanning a range of prohibited categories, providing a comprehensive testbed for assessing the generalizability of jailbreak attacks. Unlike prior work (Chen et al., 2024a; Chao et al., 2025; Andriushchenko et al., 2024), which evaluates jailbreak methods on only 50 sampled instructions, we utilize the full dataset. For training and validation, we split the 520 instructions into 364 for training and 156 for validation, ensuring that the RL agent is assessed on unseen behaviors. All baselines introduced below are trained and evaluated under the same setting.
In addition to the AdvBench benchmark, we also tested on the HarmBench (Mazeika et al., 2024) to demonstrate the robustness of the proposed TrailBlazer. HarmBench is organized into four subsets by behavioral category: Standard Behaviors, Copyright Behaviors, Contextual Behaviors, and Multimodal Behaviors. Following the prior work (Hu et al., 2025; Jha et al., 2024; Hughes et al., 2024), we evaluate on the Standard Behaviors subset of HarmBench. For testing and validation, the HarmBench splits the Standard Behaviors subset into 159 questions as the test split and 51 questions as the validation split. Our evaluation is conducted on the test split.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2]
Target LLMs.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] We evaluate our method against four contemporary LLMs to assess its performance across different architectures and developers. Unlike the baseline (Chen et al., 2024a), which focuses on the LLaMA-2 (Touvron et al., 2023) and Vicuna series as well as Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct (Jiang et al., 2024) and GPT-3.5-turbo, we validate our approach on more recent models. This choice is motivated by the fact that newer LLMs incorporate stronger safeguards compared to earlier generations, providing a more rigorous testbed to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Specifically, we experiment with three open-weight models, LLaMA-3.2-11B (Dubey et al., 2024), Qwen3-14B (Yang et al., 2025), GPT-oss-20B (Agarwal et al., 2025), and Gemma 3-12B (Team et al., 2025). For a fair comparison with the baseline, we employ the same helper LLM, GPT-3.5 Turbo.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3]
Baselines.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] To provide a comprehensive comparison, we evaluate TrailBlazer against four representative jailbreak methods that span the dominant paradigms in current research: LLM-driven search, reinforcement learning, genetic algorithms, and obfuscation.
PAIR (Chao et al., 2025) is an LLM-driven search guided by judge feedback. RLbreaker (Chen et al., 2024a) formulates the task as reinforcement learning with prompt mutators. Adaptive Attacks (Andriushchenko et al., 2024) use a model-specific prompt template and random-search an adversarial suffix when logprobs are available or transfer otherwise. AutoDAN-Turbo (Liu et al., 2024a) evolves prompts using a genetic algorithm, and FlipAttack (Liu et al., 2024b) obfuscates queries by reversing tokens.
Since PAIR, AutoDAN-Turbo, and RLbreaker require training, we train PAIR, AutoDAN-Turbo, and RLbreaker separately for each target LLM. Throughout the paper, baseline means RLbreaker.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4]
Metric.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] We evaluate all methods using two metrics: Attack Success Rate (ASR) for effectiveness and Queries Per Success (QPS) for efficiency. ASR is defined as the percentage of harmful instructions that lead to successful jailbreaks, where a response is considered successful if it fully complies with the harmful request. Following prior work (Chen et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2024b), we employ GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024) as a semantic judge to evaluate responses, rather than relying on keyword matching (Li et al., 2026). QPS is introduced by PAIR (Chao et al., 2025), which measures efficiency and is computed as the average number of queries used for successful jailbreaks. The QPS metric measures the query cost conditioned on success, and it should be interpreted together with ASR. While ASR tells us how often the attack succeeds, and QPS measures how many queries are needed when it actually does. This is crucial since a method could have a low QPS simply by succeeding very rarely, which is obviously not desirable in practice.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5]
Implementation Details.
[id=S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1] For the proposed methods, HRL and AHRL, we set the history window length to K=4K=4. For Llama 3.2-11B, to boost the performance, we used K=5K=5. Following the protocol of RLbreaker (Chen et al., 2024a), we use GPT-3.5 Turbo as the helper LLM to execute the mutator actions selected by the RL agent. Each attack episode is run for a maximum of T=5T=5 steps during training. For all baseline methods, we use their publicly available official implementations and follow the hyperparameter settings recommended in the original papers. To ensure a fair comparison at inference time, we enforce a unified query budget of 50 queries per harmful instruction. Since FlipAttack is a manual-prompt-only jailbreak method, we implement a straightforward retry protocol that repeatedly applies its fixed prompt template until a jailbreak succeeds or the 50-query budget is exhausted. Moreover, we standardize the evaluation protocol across all methods (baselines and TrailBlazer) by using GPT-4o as the judge and applying a strict 10/10 full-compliance success criterion. All experiments were conducted on a NVIDIA A6000 GPU.
[id=S4.SS2]
4.2 Discussion
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1]
Component Analysis.
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] To demonstrate the effectiveness of each component in the proposed TrailBlazer, we conduct an ablation study. As shown in Table 1, incorporating past historical embeddings through HRL alone yields substantial improvements in ASR over the baseline on both LLaMA 3.2-11B and GPT-oss-20B (e.g., from 37.18% to 60.25% and from 4.48% to 74.84%, respectively). Moreover, applying the attention-based reweighting in AHRL provides a complementary benefit of adaptive history weighting. These results support that historical information is a critical factor for jailbreak success, and that adaptively reweighting such information further enhances effectiveness.

Ablation Study on History Length.
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] In Table 2, we provide an ablation study on the effect of history length KK in TrailBlazer. Since TrailBlazer is designed to exploit vulnerabilities discovered in earlier interactions, longer history windows are expected to enhance both effectiveness and efficiency. This trend is clearly reflected in the results: while the baseline achieves only 37.18% ASR with an QPS of 21.4, incorporating even a single-step history (K=1K=1) already improves ASR to 65.38% and reduces QPS to 17.9. With K=2K=2, the ASR further jumps to 85.26% and the number of queries drops to 17.3, highlighting the benefit of integrating even short historical contexts. As KK increases, we observe continued improvements, with K=5K=5 reaching 95.51% ASR and reducing QPS to 6.3, representing a dramatic enhancement in both success rate and efficiency compared to the baseline. These results confirm that richer histories allow the agent to more effectively reweight past vulnerabilities and converge toward successful jailbreaks with fewer attempts.
We also examine the computational overhead associated with increasing KK. While larger history lengths expand the dimensionality of the historical embeddings, the additional training time remains moderate, ranging from approximately 18K to 24K seconds across different values of KK. Moreover, GPU memory consumption stays within 4500-4800MB in all settings, indicating that the approach scales efficiently without imposing prohibitive costs.
Overall, Table 2 demonstrates that even short histories yield significant performance gains, whereas longer histories further maximize efficiency without introducing substantial resource overhead.

Comparison to State-of-the-art.
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] Table 3 reports the ASR of TrailBlazer compared to four state-of-the-art jailbreak methods across four target LLMs on AdvBench. Here, TrailBlazer achieves the best ASR on all four models (LLaMA-3.2-11B, Qwen3-14B, Gemma3-12B, and GPT-oss-20B). For instance, TrailBlazer attains 95.51% on LLaMA-3.2-11B and 96.79% on Qwen3-14B, substantially outperforming the strongest baseline methods. Notably, on GPT-oss-20B, which shows relatively low baseline success rates, TrailBlazer achieves 85.30%, representing a dramatic improvement over all competitors. We interpret this as GPT-oss-20B differing from the other models in that it exhibits a higher variance in refusal rates.
As a result, memoryless jailbreaking methods often fall into repeated refusal loops when interacting with GPT-oss-20B. Once they enter a strong refusal state, they struggle to recover because they lack access to information from earlier attempts that could guide them toward more productive directions.
In contrast, the history-aware design of TrailBlazer helps the policy avoid this collapse. This demonstrates the ability of our approach to break through even models with stronger safeguards.
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1] Existing black-box methods such as PAIR, RLbreaker, AutoDAN-Turbo, Adaptive Attacks, and FlipAttack show limited success rates, especially on more robust models (e.g., only 37.18% for RLbreaker on LLaMA-3.2-11B). In contrast, TrailBlazer consistently surpasses them by a large margin, demonstrating the benefit of sequence-aware reinforcement learning.
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p3.1] While FlipAttack is appealing because it requires no training, its performance is limited by its fixed, though well-designed, prompt template. Its high ASR is largely driven by one-shot successes, which leads to favorable efficiency in terms of QPS. However, when the template fails on harder instances, simply retrying the same structure rarely changes the model’s behavior, resulting in diminishing returns. In contrast, our method uses prompt evolution and search to modify and improve prompts during the attack. It can discover stronger templates tailored to previously resistant queries and model-specific defenses, yielding more robust performance overall. This aligns with our results: In terms of ASR, TrailBlazer outperforms FlipAttack on three of four LLMs, while matching its 100% ASR on Gemma-3-12B.
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p4.1] We also evaluate our method on HarmBench to demonstrate its robustness. Here, since the publicly available HarmBench validation set contains only 41 samples while the test set contains 159 samples, we evaluated ASR on the 159 HarmBench test samples without any retraining on HarmBench. As shown in Table 4, our proposed TrailBlazer achieves a substantial improvement over the baseline (RLBreaker) on HarmBench, and the overall improvement trend is consistent with what we observe on AdvBench.
In summary, these results demonstrate that TrailBlazer not only outperforms existing black-box jailbreak methods but also establishes a new state-of-the-art in jailbreak success across diverse LLM architectures. Additional qualitative examples of successful jailbreak responses are included in the supplementary material.

Transferability.
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] To examine whether an agent trained on a specific LLM can effectively transfer to other target LLMs, we conduct the transferability experiment shown in Table 5. Here, we employed LLaMA 3.2-11B, Qwen 3-14B, GPT-oss-20B. The results indicate that TrailBlazer exhibits strong cross-model generalization in most cases. For instance, when trained on LLaMA-3.2-11B and evaluated on Qwen3-14B, our method attains an ASR of 94.87%, surpassing RLbreaker (89.10%). Similarly, training on Qwen3-14B and testing on the LLaMA-3.2-11B model yields 55.77%, again achieving better performance than RLbreaker (53.20%). When the target model is GPT-oss-20B, the overall transferability is low, yet TrailBlazer still maintains an advantage over the RLbreaker.
In addition, training on the larger GPT-oss-20B and transferring to other LLMs yields particularly strong results, such as 93.59% ASR when evaluated on LLaMA-3.2-11B and 94.87% on Qwen 3-14B. By contrast, RLbreaker exhibits weaker transfer performance in nearly all cases, with the only exception being the transfer from LLaMA 3.2-11B to GPT-oss-20B. This contrast highlights the importance of leveraging historical embeddings for robust cross-model generalization. These findings suggest that the historical reweighting mechanism in TrailBlazer enables reliable transfer of jailbreak strategies across LLMs, underscoring its potential as a practical black-box jailbreak framework in real-world scenarios.
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5]
Can MLP Learn to Choose Mutators?
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1] In the given PPO model, both the Actor and Critic networks are implemented as simple MLPs.
The Actor takes the state as input and chooses which mutator to apply next, so the network is essentially solving a small discrete action selection problem. Because we only have five mutators (e.g., rephrase, shorten, etc.), and because the state already includes the accumulated historical interaction features, the Actor is not required to model a highly complex decision boundary.
At the same time, the role of Critic network is to estimate how promising the current state is by predicting the value V(t)V^{(t)}, which represents the expected future reward from that state.
During training, the Critic is supervised to match the discounted return,
R(t)=∑k=t+1Tγk−t−1​r(k)R^{(t)}=\sum_{k=t+1}^{T}\gamma^{k-t-1}r^{(k)}, where γ\gamma and rr are discount hyperparameter and reward, respectively.
During training, we observe that the value loss gradually decreases and stabilizes, indicating that the Critic successfully learns the reward structure. The convergence graph is shown in the supplementary material.
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px6]
Defense Methods.
[id=S4.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1] Test-time defense methods against jailbreaking algorithms usually either alter the user’s prompt to disrupt common jailbreaking patterns and make the model more likely to detect the hidden harmful intention from the users (Robey et al., 2023; Kumar et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023), or focus on applying some modified decoding procedures designed to steer the generation process away from unsafe content (Li et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024). As shown in Table 6, we experiment on three defense methods: (1) prompt rephrasing and (2) a perplexity filter, and (3) self-reminder (Xie et al., 2023). The perplexity-based defense computes the GPT-2 perplexity PPL⁡(x)\mathrm{PPL}(x) of an input prompt xx and rejects xx whenever PPL⁡(x)>τ\mathrm{PPL}(x)>\tau, with τ=30\tau=30 following the protocols from RLbreaker. On the other hand, rephrasing each prompt and then issuing a second query to the target LLM is computationally expensive. Also following RLbreaking, to avoid this two-pass overhead, we implement rephrasing as a system-level instruction that combines both steps in a single call. For self-reminder, we use the provided prompts from the original paper. Overall, TrailBlazer achieves higher ASR than RLbreaker across all defense settings and backbone models, with the only exception on Gemma3-12B, where RLbreaker matches TrailBlazer in perplexity and slightly exceeds TrailBlazer in rephrasing with less than 1% of differences. Interestingly, rephrasing can increase ASR on Llama 3.2-11B for both methods compared to the no-defense setting, suggesting that naive rephrasing may act as a “prompt optimizer” that removes surface artifacts which otherwise trigger safety heuristics.
[id=S5]
5 Conclusion
[id=S5.p1.1] Limitation
While TrailBlazer achieves strong results, our method is not free from limitations. Since our framework builds upon RLbreaker, the action space remains restricted to a small set of predefined mutators, which may limit the diversity of jailbreak strategies. Extending this space with richer linguistic operations or multi-agent mechanisms could further enhance performance.
[id=S5.p2.1] Conclusion
In this work, we presented TrailBlazer, a sequence-aware history-guided reinforcement learning framework for jailbreaking large language models. Unlike prior approaches that treat each attempt independently, TrailBlazer explicitly leverages historical vulnerabilities through history-augmented reinforcement learning (HRL) and further refines this information with attention-based reweighting (AHRL). This design enables the agent to exploit critical cues from previous interactions, resulting in substantially higher attack success rates and reduced query costs.
Extensive experiments on AdvBench, Harmbench, and across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that TrailBlazer consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, TrailBlazer achieves state-of-the-art performance on all four latest LLMs, such as LLaMA-3.2-11B, Qwen3-14B, Gemma3-12B,and GPT-oss-20B. Ablation studies further confirm the effectiveness of both HRL and AHRL, as well as the efficiency gains achieved by increasing history length. In addition, transferability experiments show that TrailBlazer-trained agents generalize well across different LLM architectures, highlighting their practicality in diverse real-world scenarios.
Through this work, our findings suggest that sequence-aware RL provides a powerful paradigm for jailbreak generation. Our framework positions the model in a supporting role for paraphrasing attack prompts, while reinforcement learning leverages the weighted response history of the target LLM to govern the jailbreak process. Our experiments on AdvBench and HarmBench show that this design achieves higher or comparable jailbreak success without increasing query usage. While TrailBlazer establishes a new state-of-the-art in attack performance, future work may explore non-RL-based history-exploiting strategies, as well as extensions of TrailBlazer to broader alignment and robustness evaluations.
[id=S1a]
A Impact statement
[id=S1a.p1.1] The research presented in this paper, which details a more effective method for jailbreaking LLMs, carries inherent dual-use concerns. We acknowledge that malicious actors could misuse our TrailBlazer framework. However, our primary motivation is to create more powerful tools to proactively discover and patch security flaws for model training agencies. By exposing the critical role of interaction history in successful attacks, our work provides the AI safety community with crucial insights needed to build more robust and resilient safeguards.

A.1 Different LLM Judges
[id=A1.SS1.p1.1] Additionally, we evaluated the models using alternative LLM judges (GPT-oss and Gemini 2.5 Flash), as shown in Table 7. As expected, the ASR scores decrease when using judges other than GPT-4o. GPT-4o tends to treat responses containing indirect phrasing, partial explanations, or metaphorical wording as still conveying harmful guidance, and therefore marks them as successful attacks. Meanwhile, models such as GPT-oss and Gemini Flash are more conservative in these borderline cases. When a response remains suggestive or indirect, these judges often classify it as a failure. This results in lower ASR when using judges other than GPT-4o. In this work, to maintain consistency with prior jailbreak studies, we follow the common practice of using GPT-4o as the primary judge.

A.2 Can MLP Learn to Choose Mutators?
[id=A1.SS2.p1.1] In the given PPO model, both the Actor and Critic networks are implemented as simple MLPs.
The Actor takes the state as input and chooses which mutator to apply next, so the network is essentially solving a small discrete action selection problem. Because we only have five mutators (e.g., rephrase, shorten, etc.), and because the state already includes the accumulated historical interaction features, the Actor is not required to model a highly complex decision boundary.
At the same time, the role of Critic network is to estimate how promising the current state is by predicting the value V(t)V^{(t)}, which represents the expected future reward from that state.
During training, the Critic is supervised to match the discounted return,
R(t)=∑k=t+1Tγk−t−1​r(k)R^{(t)}=\sum_{k=t+1}^{T}\gamma^{k-t-1}r^{(k)}, where γ\gamma and rr are discount hyperparameter and reward, respectively.
During training, as shown in Fig 2, we observe that the value loss gradually decreases and stabilizes, indicating that the Critic successfully learns the reward structure.
Stable training of Critic also stabilizes the advantage estimates (A(t)=R(t)−V(t)A^{(t)}=R^{(t)}-V^{(t)}), ensuring that the Actor is updated using meaningful and consistent learning signals rather than noise.
Figure 2: Value loss during PPO training for Qwen3-14B (dark blue) and GPT-oss-20B (sky blue). Both models show fast initial decrease and stable convergence, indicating successful learning of the value function.

A.3 Details about Response Feature
[id=A1.SS3.p1.1] Regarding the response features, these are simple scalar features intended to provide coarse characteristics of the model’s output. Concretely, the four values are: (1) refusal flag ∈0,1\in{0,1}, (2) perplexity ∈[0,10]\in[0,10], (3) normalized length ∈[0,1]\in[0,1], and (4) toxicity ∈[0,1]\in[0,1]. Each feature is computed using simple heuristics: refusal flag (binary keyword matching), perplexity (token count ×0.1\times 0.1, capped at 10), normalized length (characters / 1000, capped at 1), and toxicity (proportion of five predefined toxic keywords). These features are concatenated with the prompt embedding (ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, d=1024d=1024) to form the full state vector. Here, we would like to emphasize that these features serve only as coarse indicators within the state.

A.4 Closed Source Models
[id=A1.SS4.p1.1] We initially aimed to conduct experiments on commercially widely used closed-source models, such as GPT-5.2 and Gemini. Unfortunately, during the training process using their APIs, we encountered account restriction alerts that prevented us from completing these experiments. Nevertheless, our proposed method already demonstrates substantially superior performance on the latest models and operates as a black-box framework that does not require access to the internal model architecture. We therefore expect our approach to generalize well to such closed-source settings as well.
